Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:27: And even according to the words of Rabbi Abba bar Chanina, who said there is no remedy for it, it is possible that his sin was great, along the lines of Doeg the Edomite, who, although great in Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, nevertheless called him wicked - "and to the wicked, God said, what have you to do with declaring My statutes" (Psalms 50:16) - and they said in the chapter "Chelek" (Sanhedrin 106b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Doeg, when you reach the passage of murderers and the passage of slanderers, what do you expound in them? "And you take My covenant in your mouth" - Rabbi Ami said, Doeg's Torah was only from the lips outward.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:28: Also, it is possible to resolve this, as Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, author of Menorat HaMaor, resolved it (letter 50): what it says, that there is a remedy for it, refers to one not habituated, who has a remedy so as not to continue - but one constant in the matter, "his hand still stretched out," is cut off in his sin. And it is possible to broaden his words with what Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, explained in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, letter 202), giving the reason that the slanderer's sin is greater than idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed (Arachin 15b) - he gives five reasons for the matter, one of them being that the master of the tongue's repentance is difficult, for it is possible he spoke slander about many and does not know who they are in order to appease them. Further, that from the abundance of his habit it is impossible for him to repent properly, for speaking slander has become second nature to him. For this reason we can say there is no remedy for it. And concerning something similar to this, it also says in the Zohar (Parashat Metzora, page 53a) that he has no repentance - and this is difficult, for it is written (Leviticus 14:2), "on the day of his cleansing, he shall be brought to the priest" - rather, certainly it speaks of one for whom speaking slander has become second nature, and it is impossible for him to be purified from it - and the intent of saying "he has no repentance" is that his repentance is difficult, until he repents properly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:29: And in Devarim Rabbah (Parashat Shoftim, 9) it says that in the days of Saul they did not merit the building of the Temple because there were slanderers among them, Doeg and the Ziphites. And in the days of Ahab, although they were idol-worshippers, because there was no slander among them, they were victorious in war. Further there, another interpretation: Rabbi Muna said, whoever speaks slander removes the Shechinah from below to above. Know that this is so from what David says (Psalms 57:5), "my soul is among lions, I lie among those who blaze - the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword" - what is written after it? (57:6) "be exalted above the heavens, O God," and so on. David said, Master of the universe, what is the Shechinah doing below? Remove the Shechinah to the firmament - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:30: See how severe slander is, more severe than bloodshed, forbidden relations, and idolatry - than bloodshed, as it is written (Genesis 4:13), "my iniquity is greater than can be borne"; than forbidden relations, as it is written (ibid. 39:9), "how then could I do this great evil"; than idolatry, as it is written (Exodus 32:31), "please, this people has sinned a great sin." But concerning slanderers, neither "great" [masculine] nor "greata" [feminine misuse] is written, but "great things" [plural], as it is said (Psalms 12:4), "may the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks great things" - therefore it is said (Proverbs 18:21), "death and life are in the hand of the tongue."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:31: Another interpretation: "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" - do not say, since permission has been given to me to speak, I shall say whatever I wish - the Torah has already warned you, as it is said (Psalms 34:14), "guard your tongue from evil" - and lest you say, you are causing yourself loss - no, rather you gain - and the holy spirit cries out (Proverbs 21:23), "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul [nafsho] from troubles [mitzarot]" - do not read "mitzarot" but "mi-tzara'at nafsho" [from the leprosy of his soul] - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:32: Now, in what this teaching says at its end, "from the leprosy of his soul," we find a fine resolution - for we see that many people speak slander and have no plagues or leprosy - rather, certainly the leprosy and the plague are fixed in the soul: when the soul ascends every night, all the holy ones keep away from it and proclaim concerning it that it is impure, as it says (Leviticus 13:45), "and he shall cry, unclean, unclean" - or after its departure from this world, if it did not do proper repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:33: And somewhat inclining toward this explanation are the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Parashat Ki Tazria, page 46b) - although he does not change the word "mitzarot" from its plain meaning, nevertheless from the general matter something is heard along the lines of what is being expounded, in these words, on the verse (Genesis 2:7), "and man became a living soul" - he explains there that "a living soul" is the neshamah, which is the highest level among the levels of holiness in man. And he says afterward: come and see, at every time this holy soul cleaves to a person, he is beloved of his Master, how many guards guard him from every side, he is marked for good above and below, and the holy Shechinah rests upon him - but at the time he strays from his ways, the Shechinah withdraws from him, and the holy soul does not cleave to him, and from the side of the strong evil serpent this spirit is aroused, which roams and goes through the world, for it rests only in a place from which supernal holiness has withdrawn - and then the person is defiled and blemished in his flesh, in the appearance of his face, in everything.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:34: And come and see, because this living soul is holy, supernal - when the holy land [i.e., Malchut] draws it within itself and it is included, then we call it neshamah, and this is what ascends above and speaks before the holy King, and enters all gates, and none can stop its hand - and therefore it is called "the speaking spirit," for all other souls have no permission to speak before the King except this one. And therefore the Torah proclaimed and said, "guard your tongue from evil," and so on, and it is written, "he who guards his mouth and his tongue" - because if his lips and his tongue speak evil words, those words ascend above, and at the time they ascend, all proclaim and say, clear away from around the evil word of so-and-so, make room for the path of the strong serpent - then the holy soul is removed from him and withdraws and cannot speak, as it is said (Psalms 39:3), "I was mute with silence, I held my peace" - and that soul ascends in shame, in the distress of everything, and they do not give it a place as before - and therefore it is written, "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles" - "his soul" certainly, that which used to speak became silent because of the evil speech, and then the serpent is summoned, for everything returns to its place. And when that evil word ascends by known paths and stands before the strong serpent, how many spirits are aroused in the world, and a spirit descends from that side and finds that this person has been aroused with an evil word, and behold, the holy speaking spirit has departed from him, and then it rests upon him and defiles him, and then he becomes "closed up" [i.e., leprous].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:35: Just as this person's punishment is because of the evil word, so his punishment is for a good word that comes to his hand and he could speak it, because he blemishes that speaking spirit - for it was prepared to speak above and to speak below, and all in holiness - all the more so if a nation walks in a crooked path and he could speak to them and stays silent and does not speak, as I have said, "I was mute with silence, I held my peace, [even] from good, and my pain was stirred" (Psalms 39:3, adapted), with the plagues of impurity - and this is what King David said concerning this, "I was struck and turned away from Him," as it is written (Psalms 86:16), "turn to me and be gracious to me," as it is said (Numbers 12:10), "and Aaron turned" - to this point. And we have learned from this teaching how great is the punishment of slander.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:36: In Parashat "this shall be the law of the leper," at its beginning, in these words: Rabbi Chiya said, whoever utters slander, all his limbs are defiled, and he shall appear to need to be shut in [as a leper], because that evil word ascends and arouses an impure spirit and it becomes defiled - it comes to be defiled, they defile him - through a word below, another word is aroused.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:37: Further there, Rabbi Yehudah said, "this shall be the law of" - certainly, corresponding to this, to exact punishment from him, "the one who brings forth an evil name" - "on the day of his cleansing, he shall be brought to the priest" - what does this teach us? It implies that whoever has slander, his prayer does not enter before the Holy One, blessed be He, for an impure spirit has been aroused against him. Once he returns in repentance and accepts repentance upon himself, what is written? "On the day of his cleansing, he shall be brought to the priest" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:38: And it says, "once he returns in repentance" and "accepts repentance" - for two kinds of repentance are needed: the first, immediate repentance, which is submission, as they explained, of blessed memory (Proverbs 15:4), "a healing tongue is a tree of life, but perversity in it is a break in the spirit" - and therefore the Torah commanded hyssop, which indicates lowliness and submission. And further, "accepts repentance upon himself" - meaning, to accept upon himself not to return again to that sin, as it says (Psalms 85:9), "and let them not return to folly."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:39: And included in the repentance needed for slander is that he make himself mute concerning worldly matters, as though he had no tongue - for concerning the master of the tongue it is said (Psalms 12:4), "may the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks great things" - and the intent of "cut off" is explained as meaning that his tongue is cut off in Gehinnom as many times as he spoke slander, along the lines of what is done for other transgressions, that the limb with which he sinned is judged until all that evil he did is digested - and therefore he must cut off his own tongue from speaking while still alive, and suffer in exchange for what he enjoyed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:40: And after we have spoken of the punishment of slander, let us speak of the parts of slander - and although we have not written everything found in the words of our Rabbis, so as not to be lengthy, this reminder is enough for the wise to arouse his heart to repent. And I saw fit to condense the words of Rabbeinu Yonah in the Gate of Repentance and the other authors who write on this matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:41: The first part of slander, concerning which we were commanded in the Torah not to speak it and not to accept it, as it is said (Exodus 23:1), "you shall not accept a false report" - its essence is one who speaks disparagingly of his fellow, even if he speaks the truth - for if he speaks falsely, he is found to bring forth an evil name. And one who speaks disparagingly of his fellow intends to make his reputation stink and disgrace him, and therefore reveals the abominations of his ancestors, even if not in his presence - and this is the group of true slanderers. If he was a penitent and one speaks of his earlier sins, whether not in his presence or in his presence, his punishment is great, for one who repents has his sins made into merits, and this shames him, and it is not fitting. And further, others who hear this shame of a penitent will refrain and not repent - and it is found that he closes the door of repentance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:42: And Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, wrote that in one respect the sin of one who speaks slander about a true matter is greater than one who speaks a false matter - for people will believe what he says about his fellow to be honest words, and his stench will rise before them, and he will be despised in their eyes, even if he regretted his sin and repented - his blemish shall remain in people's mouths. And if a person sees his fellow transgress a matter of Torah in secret, he should not reveal his sin publicly, for perhaps he repented - especially if he is a single witness, for one who testifies alone against his fellow, they give him stripes for rebellion - and it is not fitting to reveal it except to a discreet sage who will not tell the rest of the masses - and if he knows they will believe him like the words of two witnesses, then he may tell it, so that that sage hate him - so they said in "Arvei Pesachim" (113b) - but it is permitted to distance oneself from his company and hate him until one knows that he has turned from his evil way.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:43: And concerning matters between a person and his fellow, such as theft, oppression, and fraud, he may tell these matters to people, for they said, of blessed memory (Ketubot 87b), that one witness obligates him to an oath. And if the sinner is a Torah scholar and a God-fearing man, it is fitting to think of him that he truly repented, as they explained, of blessed memory (Berachot 19a), "if you saw a Torah scholar commit a transgression by day, do not think ill of him at night, for he certainly repented." And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Tikkunei Zohar, page 141b), that concerning this it is said (Deuteronomy 21:23), "his corpse shall not remain overnight on the tree" - concerning the corpse of the sin he committed on the Tree of Life, for he certainly repented. And concerning this we find that Joseph the righteous was punished for bringing an evil report of his brothers to his father, and so they said in Bereshit Rabbah (84:7) on the verse (Genesis 37:2), "and Joseph brought," as Rashi explains, and for all three [reports] he was struck.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:44: But a man whom we know to be completely wicked, with no fear of God before his eyes, it is permitted to publicize him and speak disparagingly of him, to make transgressors stink in people's eyes, so that the souls of the listeners be disgusted by evil deeds - as it is said (Proverbs 8:13), "the fear of the LORD is to hate evil" - and they said, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 52a), a wicked man son of a righteous man - one may call him "wicked son of wicked"; a righteous man son of a wicked man - one may call him "righteous son of righteous."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:45: Now, if you see a person who speaks a word or does a deed that can be judged toward good or toward merit, if he is God-fearing you are obligated to judge him favorably, even if the matter leans more toward guilt. And if he is among the intermediate ones, who are careful of sin but sometimes stumble in it, you should tip the doubt to decide in his favor, as they said (Shabbat 127b), "whoever judges his fellow favorably, the Holy One, blessed be He, judges him favorably" - and it is a positive commandment from the Torah (Leviticus 19:15), "in righteousness shall you judge your fellow." And if the matter leans toward guilt, and it is like a doubt, you should decide it toward guilt. And if that man's deeds are mostly evil, or you have tested that there is no fear of God in his heart, decide his deeds and words toward guilt.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:46: And included in this group, that of speaking true slander, is one who mentions to himself alone the evil deeds of his ancestors - behold, he transgresses what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 25:17), "and you shall not wrong one another" - Scripture speaks of wronging with words. If he tells the deeds of his ancestors before others, concerning this our Rabbis said (Bava Metzia 58b), that one who shames his fellow publicly is like one who sheds blood, and descends to Gehinnom and does not ascend. Therefore a person must be careful to distance himself from speaking of people's blemishes and their disgrace, for a person's speech testifies about him and about the hidden matters within him - for the worthy person speaks of people's praises and does not wish to speak of their disgrace, but the unfit person's whole desire is to speak of people's blemishes, for because he himself is unfit he wishes to disqualify others - as we read in Kiddushin (70a): it was taught, whoever disqualifies [others], disqualifies with his own blemish, and does not speak in the world's praise - and Shmuel said, he disqualifies with his own blemish. And if the blemish is well known about him and his family, he must be even more careful to guard his tongue from mentioning it in any manner, even by hint - as they said, of blessed memory, in the chapter "HaZahav" (Bava Metzia 59b), concerning "for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:20).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:47: And included in slander is one who speaks it in a manner of jest and levity, meaning that he does not speak out of hatred - and this is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 26:18), "like a madman who shoots firebrands, arrows, and death, so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, was I not joking?" And likewise one who speaks by way of hints, that he tells it in innocence as though he did not know this matter is slander, but when protested against, says, I did not know this was so-and-so's doing. Also, be careful not to speak slander about charity collectors who are honest, and one who speaks slander about them, saying they steal and show favoritism to whomever they wish - for this slander there is no comparable punishment, for he shames the servants of the LORD and their children and relatives, and prevents good people from performing commandments, and perhaps charity collectors will come who do not do the matter properly [out of discouragement].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:48: The second part: going about as a talebearer - and we are warned about this in the Torah (Leviticus 19:16), "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people" - and it is included in the group of slanderers, as they said, of blessed memory (Bamidbar Rabbah 19:2), concerning Doeg the Edomite, that he was a master of slander and a talebearer who carried tales - for a talebearer is called one who carries words from this one to that one, "so-and-so said such-and-such about you, he did such-and-such," like this peddler who goes about the towns.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:49: And included in talebearing is being careful about what they said, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 29a): it was taught, from where do we know that a judge should not say, I would acquit but my colleagues obligate, what can I do since they are the majority? Therefore it is said, "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:50: And the talebearer magnifies hatred, and is found to destroy the pillar of the world, which is peace (Avot, chapter 1, mishnah 17). And they said, of blessed memory (Niddah 61a), concerning the matter of talebearing, that although it is forbidden to accept it and hate one's fellow because of it, one should not disdain the matter entirely, but should guard his soul and be wary of the words - and the proof is from Gedaliah ben Achikam, who, because he did not heed accepting slander at all, was killed, as they explained, of blessed memory (ibid.). And they said, of blessed memory (Devarim Rabbah 5:9), that the generation of Saul had among them stirrers of strife, like Doeg and the Ziphites, and although they were righteous, they would go down to war and fall; the generation of Ahab, who had no informers among them, would go down to war and be victorious - for Obadiah hid a hundred prophets and no one revealed it, even though Ahab and his generation were idol-worshippers.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:51: And one who stirs up strife between brothers and friends, and brings hatred between them, is more severe than all the parts of slander, along the lines of what is said (Proverbs 6:19), "and one who sows discord among brothers" - and our Rabbis said (Vayikra Rabbah 16:1) that the seventh [of the seven abominations listed] is more severe than all of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:52: Also included in talebearing is not to reveal his fellow's secret, and it is forbidden - for they said in Yoma, first chapter (4b), from where do we know that if one tells his fellow a matter, it is under "you shall not reveal it," that it is forbidden to reveal it? As it is said (Leviticus 1:1), "and the LORD spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, saying" [implying "do not repeat"]. And whoever reveals a secret departs from the way of modesty - and it appears to me that concerning this it is said, "a talebearer reveals secrets" - meaning, one who reveals secrets is called a talebearer, and he has a punishment just like an actual talebearer, being of the four groups [i.e., extended to a fifth].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:53: The third part: the dust of slander - for they said, of blessed memory, in Bava Batra (165a), that all stumble in the dust of slander - and this has four parts. The first, one who speaks excessively of his fellow's good qualities, for from his good qualities [being mentioned] comes his misfortune - so they said in the chapter "Yesh BeArachin" (16a). And Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, explained (Gate 3, letter 226), that this means he speaks of his fellow's good qualities in the presence of his enemy, and there is no one present at that gathering to protest to the enemy and blunt his teeth - but if he praises a worthy person known for piety, even if an enemy is present, he may praise him, for everyone knows the enemy is lying in his words. And it appears to me that even though one speaks of his fellow's good qualities, he should not speak of them excessively, such as things people will not believe, but only speak of matters and virtues that are believable.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:54: And included in the dust of slander is one who says, where are there coals if not in so-and-so's house, which always roasts meat (Arachin 15b). Further included in this is one who lodges in his fellow's house and is treated well by him, and the next day goes out to the marketplace and says, blessed be so-and-so, who slaughtered such-and-such and prepared such-and-such, and the like - concerning this it is said (Proverbs 27:14), "he who blesses his neighbor with a loud voice," and so on, "it shall be counted a curse to him" - for once the matter is heard, worthless people gather to the host and he loses his money on worthless guests (Arachin 16a). It appears to me that also included in this is: if a person lends his poor fellow a dinar, the poor man should not praise him, for perhaps the host's mind does not agree with everyone, and he might come to a loss, since perhaps they will not repay him properly - and one must be careful.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:55: Included in the dust of slander is what they said in the Talmud there (Arachin 15b), in these words: Rava said, any matter said in the presence of the subject involves no slander. Abaye said to him, all the more so is it brazenness and slander! He said to him, I hold like Rabbi Yosi, who said, in all my days I have never said something and then retracted it - meaning, I never said anything about a person not in his presence that I did not [also] say to his face, in his presence. But if he speaks of one who sinned, and did not first inform the sinner privately and rebuke him, it is accounted to him as slander, for he appears to flatter him [to his face] while revealing his blemish to others not in his presence, and further, they will say of him that he does not speak truth. But if he rebuked him and he did not heed him, then he may inform people of his sin, and they will not suspect him of wishing to cast aspersions on his fellow. And likewise, if the speaker is well known among the many not to show favoritism, and everything he says not in someone's presence he says in their presence, and it is established that he speaks only truth, then it is permitted for him to say those things.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:56: Further it says there, Rabbah bar Rav Huna said, any matter said in the presence of three involves no slander - why? Because your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend [so it will spread regardless]. However, if the matter said in the presence of three, or even in the presence of many, was said in confidence, it is forbidden to reveal it - and so they said in Sanhedrin (31a): that student who revealed a matter said in the study hall after twenty-two years, and Rabbi Meir expelled him from the study hall and said, this one reveals secrets - to this point. Also included in the dust of slander, Rambam wrote (Hilchot De'ot, chapter 7, halachah 3), that one should not say, be silent about so-and-so, I do not wish to say what I know about him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:57: The fourth part is the complainer, and concerning him King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 18:8), "the words of a complainer are like wounds" - and a complainer is a man whose way is to complain and grumble about his fellow, and voice complaints from his heart, saying, so-and-so said such-and-such to me, and his intent was only to insult me, and he intended me harm, even though he intended his good - and he multiplies complaints, and presents himself as oppressed, as though people rob him and insult him and curse him for nothing - and concerning this it is written (Proverbs 16:28), "and a complainer separates close friends" - meaning, he separates from himself a friend and companion. And whoever has this evil quality, just as he complains about people, so he hurls words toward Heaven, and thinks concerning the kindness of the Name that His intent is to take vengeance on His creatures and bring calamity to the world - and even if he sees a bestowal of good, he says it will turn out badly in the end - as it is said (Deuteronomy 1:27), "and you complained in your tents and said, because the LORD hates us," and so on - and our Sages, of blessed memory, said, do not multiply complaints, lest you come to sin. And the complainer, in his evil nature, is ungrateful, for he thinks the good things done for him are evil, and repays evil for good. And this evil quality comes from an evil heart, for from his evil heart he sees a person's good as evil, and brings his evil thought into action, speaking evil and complaining.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:58: The fifth part concerns vulgarity of the mouth, and Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor (letter 56), in these words: we find that many people are forced with whips, fire, and water, and every kind of coercion, to confess matters for which they are guilty, and they endure all the coercion and do not confess anything with their mouths that would obligate them, through their confession, to execution - and even though they see that it is only a temporary death, for they know for certain that today or tomorrow they will die anyway, nevertheless, in order to gain a temporary life, they endure their distress and accept all the sufferings in the world. All the more so, one who is not forced to say vulgar words, and has no pleasure in this speech, but knows that in saying it, "his iniquity is greater than can be borne," and he shall be judged with everlasting death for it - he should have shut and stopped his mouth from saying it, for whoever speaks vulgarly, his sentence is turned against him for evil - as we read in the first chapter of Ketubot (8b): "therefore the LORD shall not rejoice over their young men," and so on (Isaiah 9:16) - and what is "and His hand is still stretched out"? Rav Chanan bar Abba said, everyone knows why a bride enters the wedding canopy [i.e., for marital relations] - but whoever speaks vulgarly and brings forth a vulgar word from his mouth, even if a decree of seventy good years was sealed for him, it is turned against him for evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:59: And we also read in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 33a): because of the sin of vulgarity of the mouth, many troubles and evils and harsh decrees are renewed in the world, and the young men of the enemies of Israel [euphemism] die, and orphans and widows cry out and are not answered, as it is said, "therefore the LORD shall not rejoice over their young men," and so on. What is "and His hand is still stretched out"? Rav Chanan said, and so on. And Rav Chisda said, whoever speaks vulgarly, they deepen his Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 22:14), "a deep pit is the mouth of strange women [or: strangers]." Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] says, even one who hears and stays silent, as it is said, "he with whom the LORD is angry shall fall there."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:60: Therefore a person must purify his mouth from speaking vulgarity, for the holy mouth was created only to speak holiness - and one who speaks vulgarly abandons the way of shame and modesty, which are the choice qualities by which Israel are distinguished from the other nations, and shows about himself that he has no share in the holy nation - to this point. And I have shortened some of it so as not to be lengthy. And so Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Sha'arei Teshuvah (Gate 3, letter 229).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:61: And concerning the punishment of one who soils his mouth, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Pekudei, page 249b) in the palaces of holiness, third palace, in these words: these are four who stand and lend and excommunicate all those who bring forth from their mouths an unnecessary word and soil their mouths - and these excommunicate him, and he remains for forty days during which his prayer is not heard and does not enter the curtain, and he remains rebuked outside - to this point. Behold, he is rebuked and excommunicated, and for forty days his prayer does not ascend above. And it says further there, whoever is excommunicated above, his Maker's protection withdraws from him, and his soul does not ascend above - and we shall copy the rest of his wording below.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:62: Further, in the palaces of impurity (ibid., page 263b), in one palace, in these words: and from this evil spirit hang several other bands, appointed to seize an evil word or a filthy word that a person utters from his mouth, and afterward utters holy words - woe to them, woe to their lives - these are the people who cause those other bands to rule and to blemish a holy place - woe to them in this world, woe to them in the World to Come, for these impure spirits take this impure word, and when a person afterward utters a holy word, these impure spirits get there first and take that impure word and defile that holy word, and the person gains nothing from it, and, as it were, the holy power is weakened - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:63: And further, they said, of blessed memory (Derech Eretz Rabbah, chapter 3): Rabbi Elazar said, a handsome, praiseworthy person who brings forth a disgraceful word from his mouth - to what is he comparable? To a beautiful hall with a tanner's drainpipe fixed in it - every passerby says, how beautiful this hall is, except that a tanner's drainpipe is in it - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:64: The sixth part: that he not bring forth a disgraceful word from his mouth - and although they said, a person should always teach his students in a concise manner, it is better to be a bit lengthy so as not to bring forth a disgraceful word from one's mouth - as we read in the first chapter of Pesachim (3a): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a person should never bring forth a disgraceful word from his mouth, for Scripture went out of its way for eight letters rather than bring forth a disgraceful word from its mouth, as it is said (Genesis 7:8), "and of the animals that are not clean" [rather than saying "impure"]. Rav Ashi said, nine [letters], as it is said (Deuteronomy 23:11), "if there is among you a man who is not clean, because of a nocturnal emission." Rav said, sixteen [letters], as it is said (1 Samuel 20:26), "for he said, something has happened to him, he is not clean, surely he is not clean." And they elaborated further there. And it further says there: there were three priests, one said, my portion came to me doubled (explained as referring to the showbread), one said, my portion came to me the size of an olive, and one said, the size of a lizard's tail - they investigated him and found a taint of disqualification in him - it follows that a person's speech testifies about him and about his root.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:65: And the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Submission, chapter 6) wrote, in these words: and it is said of one of the pious ones who passed by a very foul-smelling dog carcass, and his students said to him, how foul-smelling is this carcass! He said to them, how white are its teeth! And they regretted having spoken of its disgrace. And since it is disgraceful to speak of a dead dog, all the more so of a living person - and since it is good to praise a dog's carcass for the whiteness of its teeth, all the more so is it an obligation, by this reasoning, to praise a wise person. And his intent was to rebuke them for not training their tongue to speak evil, lest it become their nature - and so, when they train their tongue to speak good, it shall become their fixed nature, as it is written (Psalms 15:3), "he has no slander on his tongue" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:66: The seventh part: not to give his fellow a bad nickname - for they said, of blessed memory, in Bava Metzia (58b): all descend to Gehinnom and ascend, except these, who descend and do not ascend, and these are: one who gives his fellow a bad nickname, one who shames his fellow publicly, and one who has relations with a married woman. Is giving a nickname the same as shaming? [The Talmud answers:] it is necessary [to state both], for even though [the fellow] is accustomed to being called by that name [it is still forbidden] - to this point. Behold, they equated one who gives a bad nickname with one who has relations with a married woman, which is among the severe transgressions for which one must be killed rather than transgress.
